text.p: New Zealand retailer Progressive Enterprises Ltd said on Monday its 81 percent fall in annual net profit was "completely unsatisfactory" but it aimed to restore an acceptable level of profit through a series of recent initiatives.

Progressive said consolidated operating profit fell to $3.55 million from $19.09 million a year earlier. The result was after $2.047 million of redundancy costs, including the restructuring of the Foodtown and Countdown management teams, and plant and equipment writeoffs of $1.309 million.
Progressive said the result also included special incentive income of $1.26 million and profit arising from property sales of $1.52 million.
It blamed a number of factors for its poor result, including softer retail sales and competition in the discount sector in the early part of the year.

Georgie Pie restaurants suffered significantly higher losses due to competition, volume declines, the transfer of stores to franchisees and additional costs associated with the new manufacturing plant and restaurant openings.
Progressive said it failed to control gross profit margins in some produce and meat operations in the first half of the year. One of its operations failed to contain store wage costs in that period.
Head office costs rose due to the inability of the financial, merchandising and operational systems to adequately meet changing business requirements.
Higher interest rates were also a factor.
Since year-end, Progressive had signed a conditional contract with McDonalds for the transfer of up to 17 of the Georgie Pie restaurants.
The company said this and other initiatives should "substantially assist in restoring the Group's profitability to a more acceptable level in the new financial year".
Fund manager PDFM earlier disclosed a 5.3 percent interest in Progressive in a notice to the New Zealand Stock Exchange. PDFM and UBS International Investment London jointly hold 6.965 percent.
Progressive is 57 percent owned by Foodland Associated . -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
